title: Tuck Everlasting
full_review:
"Tuck Everlasting" (Disney) is a charming, fairy-tale fantasy about a young girl's first love and how she is tempted by him to live a life staying forever young.

Set at the turn of the last century, two families inhabit the environs of Treefall: the prosperous Fosters, who helped build the town, and the nomadic Tuck family, who have come and gone over the years.

The Fosters (Victor Garber and Amy Irving) reside in a grand, gated house and live a cultured life of privilege, propriety and property, which they expect their only daughter, Winnie (Alexis Bledel), to assume. The Tucks, led by spooky Angus (William Hurt) and kind Mae (Sissy Spacek), with their two sons, the zestful Jesse (Jonathan Jackson) and older, brooding Miles (Scott Bairstow), are a clan of wanderers who camp out in the wilderness forest that is part of the Foster estate.

The Tucks have a family secret. A hundred years ago, as pioneers, they discovered a virtual fountain of youth in the spring waters of a tree stump on the Fosters' land. Not only do they stay young, but the waters make them impervious to death and even injury. Ostracized by an earlier generation as devil worshippers, they now keep only to themselves, but must periodically return to the Foster estate to drink the waters and thus preserve their immortality.

Tracking the Tucks across the country is a mysterious Man in a Yellow Suit, played with eerie slyness by Sir Ben Kingsley. He has heard of the Tuck legend passed down through the generations and now is bound and determined to find the elusive Tucks. "One must never announce one's presence to the prey," he warns.

When Winnie's parents decide she needs the discipline of a girls' boarding school, she flees into the adjoining forest where she stumbles upon young Jesse Tuck drinking water from a tree stump. Before he can show Winnie the way back home, brother Miles drags Winnie back to the Tuck homestead. At first suspicious, the Tucks soon take Winnie into their trust and open her eyes to the beauty of the natural world just beyond the gates of her house, all the while offering to return her home. Before long Winnie falls in love with Jesse and forgets that she ever wanted to leave.

Meanwhile, the Fosters have the whole town out looking for Winnie and it is The Man in the Yellow Suit who becomes pivotal in Winnie's fate when he spies her on a lake with Angus. Soon she must make a crucial decision about how and with whom she wishes to live her life.

Based on Natalie Babbitt's novel and directed by Jay Russell, the uplifting tale has enough twists, turns and excitement to keep both young and older audiences in suspense. The film does a fine job of storytelling with a stellar, Academy Award-winning cast and some very good newcomers. Added to that are idyllic period sets and costuming that are the Disney trademark, a musical score which evokes the carefree spirit of Celtic leprechauns, and lush cinematography that nicely captures the scenic outdoors and warm interior details.

For the most part, it is a gentle tale that also visits the perennial question of how to preserve the natural world pristinely against the manmade forces of commerce and civilization. Yet one must remember the movie is a fantasy lest it present a confusing and false idea of the world to younger, impressionable minds. While it does not fully endorse a childish Peter Pan-like existence, it does depict immortality as resulting from the animistic forces of "nature" as opposed to Christian beliefs in God and his salvation that leads to eternal life after death. As a period fantasy piece, however, "Tuck" has genuine appeal and hopefully will have a long life at the box office.

Due to some violence, mild sexual innuendo and its fantasy interpretation of immortality, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
